title: Re: A reimagined OS with no folders and no apps...
text:
I honestly think we should not make computers even more "magical" and difficult to understand than they already are.

I also never understood what OS vendors have against files and folders. It was one of the metaphors that caught on really well with non-technical users and allowed them to establish their own ordering system, much like you would establish a system in your home.

I feel that removing this and forcing everything into a flat space is contributing to clutter and chaos, not reducing it.

I'd like to know how this OS would answer the simple question "where is my data, what is stored on this device?"

Oh and also of course: What does this OS do if Claude is offline?

title: Re: Turbo Vision-style UI for Claude Code...
text:
We (Claude and I) built a Turbo Vision UI for Claude Code / Claude Code sessions. It's a quick experiment so your mileage may vary and PRs welcome.

What is Turbo Vision? It's the old school DOS interface that a lot of people like me programmed with in high school in environments like Borland Turbo Pascal and Turbo C. It's very nostalgic for some of us.

This system will remember the windows/tiles you have set up when you go back in.

title: Show HN: What HN community recommended learning in 2026
text:
Hi HN!

I've been software engineer for about 15 years. For me this industry was always about learning. To be honest, I don't feel this anymore. I see more and more people delegating most of their work to LLMs. We rarely talk about software design or architecture, because Claude is such a great companion, so most of the workers don't need these technical discussions.

Sometimes I feel a bit lost. I am not sure, what should I learn to stay in the industry and to have opportunity to work on interesting problems.

I always saw HN as a place full of ambitious and creatives people. Inspired by hackertube.org and hackerbooks.org, I scanned HN comments in 2026 to extract learning materials recommended by community here, to help me decide with the next steps in my learning journey.

Best, Mateusz

title: Show HN: A terminal-native idle factory game, written in Rust with ratatui
text:
Hey HN readers!

I'm snipedbywifi (https://gitlab.com/snipedbywifi), and i've been working on terminactory. Please try it out if you'd like to play a cozy factory game while waiting for long agent tasks to finish!

The game is a factory game (overused niche, i know xD), but runs in your terminal. Reason i built it? glad you asked: So basically, it started off with me wanting a terminal-native factory game. Me and the modern 5.5 claude models made a base for the game that I liked, and then i went ham adding features / fixing some minor flaws (like adding claude code hooks so you recieve "telegrams" [the agent's responses], so you can review progress directly in-game). (yes, I had heavy AI assistance, disclaimer!!!)

Right now, the game has basic factory features you'd expect from a game like this (build stuff, delete stuff, measure how much you're earning, basic selection tools), along with a few more.. "unexpected" features. This includes a fake in-game browser that has a wiki, fake forums, some fun bits of lore, some more lore, a LOT more lore, and a research graph that shows how many items or how much RP (research points) you'd need to unlock something, and some more QOL features.

If anyone actually has this issue / want of a terminal-based game that runs alongside your agents so you don't doomscroll, do you have any suggestions, or additional ideas I could add?

It's hosted on GitLab, soo, that's one additional thing i'd like to mention

Thanks for reading!! snipedbywifi

(p.s. first HN post lol) (p.s. p.s. there's a lot of hidden lore in the game, so.. lore-divers? you might like it?)

title: Show HN: Yet another agent manager (but we needed it)
text:
Hello HN,

I am Ioannis and I would like to introduce Logonomic, a desktop application we made to help us work with LLM CLIs (e.g. codex, claude, opencode etc) in a more organized way. It runs the CLIs already installed, with their existing accounts and configuration and organizes sessions by repository. It is available for Windows and Linux, with a preview for macOS. There is also a mobile companion app, to work remotely (Android and soon iOS too).

We built it originally to assist us in our own work, to address the common case of multiple agents running concurrently in many repositories. It was hard to keep track of what each one is doing and which one needs attention or requires action.

There are many tools by now broadly that broadly target the same problem. This one is a native C++/Qt application with our own terminal emulator. Some of its features:

- An 'overview' mode that shows all running sessions, optionally grouped by repository, each with its status, title and summary that the agents update regularly.

- Agents add a trailer to their commits, enabling to re-open the conversations that produced them.

- Terminals run in their own processes and survive UI crashes.

- A plot that shows line counts over time, by directory or language, where clicking on a sample brings up the corresponding commit in the git log.

- A treemap that shows how the repo's files are organized, with a diff mode that colours changed files, whose diff opens with a double click.

- Token usage and remaining account quotas shown where available, with usage broken down by day and repository.

- Sessions can exchange messages (1:1 or broadcast), may hand tasks to each other or continue other session's work.

The supported CLIs are Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, Antigravity, Grok Build, Kimi Code and Qwen Code.

The free edition has no time limit and runs up to four terminals. The paid editions have perpetual one-time licences from €150 for 2 seats and include 12 months of feature updates, no terminal limit, GitHub/GitLab CI integrations, as well as an Android companion app (iOS will follow).

The application itself is proprietary. Many of its core components are open source, among them the terminal emulator and the plotting library: https://github.com/Varinomics

This is the first public release, so there will be rough edges, and we would like to hear about them.
author: imakris

title: Re: The Claude Delusion...
text:
People on the author's side of this debate just haven't seen the firsthand evidence yet. I can understand being skeptical until then, but they owe it to themselves to give late-2026 frontier models a try.

The lightbulb moment for me was when I gave Claude Code a tough reverse-engineering problem: understanding how a complex, proprietary encoding scheme worked, then building an encoder and decoder. There are some additional complicating factors that I can't disclose, because this was for work, but it was a tough problem.

For context, I've been doing RE for over 25 years. I'm not the best in the world, but I'm pretty good at it when I can find the time.

A coworker and I had spent about a week on the work, and I estimated it would take us another 2-3 to complete the work. We had figured out how about 3/4 of the messages were encoded, but the rest just didn't make sense.

I gave Claude Code our notes, and in 15 minutes it had finished figuring out the rest of the protocol and built a command-line decoder. I asked it to add an encoding feature, and in another ten minutes, it had done that as well. It tested all of its own code extensively using our corpus of real data.

The decoder worked perfectly on all of our existing captures as well as new data collected after that.

I had to make a small change to the encoder that was related to one of the things I can't disclose. I don't hold that against the model, because it didn't have access to the real product to test its output against. Making the change took maybe an hour because there was some trial-and-error involved.

That kind of capability is a genuine game-changer, especially when the interface is "describe the result you want in natural language". Ten years ago, I would have thought a truly useful natural language interface to a complex system was 20 to 30 years away at best.

Being able to quickly clone nearly all of the functionality of Adobe's entire product suite is another favourite example of mine.

This is by far the most disruptive technology I've seen introduced in my lifetime. A lot of people are using it for questionable purposes, but that always happens when people are figuring out how to make the best use of something new.

title: Re: GR00T 2: new World-Action Model (WAM) from Nvidia...
text:
nvidia's new WAM is impressive: It needs very few demonstrations ("Zero-shot generalization and few-shot adaptation"), and self improvement with RL on the real robot increases task success rate.

Finally, a new architecture emerges: a (cloud) frontier model in agentic mode orchestrates the full robot. This was already demonstrated in [1] and may be the reason why openai closes its robotics department [2].
